nameStory: The Mower's Mushroom earned its name because it pops up on freshly cut lawns, seemingly appearing overnight after you've run the mower over your grass. It's also called the haymaker's mushroom because it fruits during traditional haying season when farmers would cut and gather their grass crops. This little brown fungus has a knack for timing its appearance with our lawn care routines!
description: Mower's Mushroom is one of the most common little brown mushrooms you'll encounter on New England lawns and grassy areas. These small, unassuming fungi have brownish caps that start bell-shaped when young and flatten out as they mature. They typically grow to about 1-3 inches tall with caps reaching 1-2 inches across. Despite being everywhere underfoot, they're not edible and belong to a group called mottlegills due to their distinctive speckled gill pattern.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: The gills start pale gray but develop a distinctive mottled or speckled appearance as dark spores mature unevenly, creating patches of light and dark areas that give this mushroom its 'mottlegill' nickname

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Brownish cap starts bell-shaped when young, flattening with age, often with a slightly darker center and lighter edges that may fade to tan or buff color

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thin, fragile stem that's hollow inside and easily snaps when bent, usually the same color as the cap or slightly paler

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Dark brown to black spore print that you can see by placing the cap gill-side down on white paper overnight

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, earthy smell with no distinctive or unpleasant odors when crushed or bruised

habitat: Look for Mower's Mushrooms in well-maintained lawns, parks, golf courses, and other grassy areas throughout New England. They particularly love nutrient-rich soil where grass clippings decompose, and you'll often spot them in the same spots year after year. They're saprophytic fungi, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in the soil rather than forming partnerships with tree roots.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in late spring when soil warms and moisture levels are right, often after spring rains and the first few lawn mowings of the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when they're most abundant, popping up regularly after rain showers and lawn watering, especially in July and August.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting into early fall as long as temperatures remain mild and there's adequate moisture, but become less common as nights get cooler.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant during New England winters, with no visible fruiting bodies present above ground.

funFact: These mushrooms can complete their entire life cycle from spore to spore-producing adult in just 24-48 hours under perfect conditions, which is why they seem to magically appear overnight on your freshly mowed lawn!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small brown lawn mushrooms, but the mottled gill pattern is your best identifying feature - look for those distinctive light and dark patches on the gills that other common lawn mushrooms don't have. Remember: "Mottled gills mean mottlegills!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "mushroom" and looking harmless, never eat Mower's Mushrooms or any wild fungi without expert identification. Some related species contain compounds that can cause unpleasant effects, and proper identification requires microscopic examination of spores.
compareHints: Mower's Mushroom differs from its mottlegill relatives by its preference for grassy lawns rather than dung (like Shiny Mottlegill) or its smaller size compared to Banded Mottlegill. Unlike Petticoat Mottlegill, it lacks the distinctive ring around the stem and has a more subdued brown coloration rather than striking black and white patterns.
